title: How to work fractional cross-stitches together
subtitle: Combining quarter and three-quarter stitches in the same square
excerpt: Fractional stitches share a square when a chart calls for two different colours or values to blend at a curved edge. A quarter cross-stitch and a three-quarter cross-stitch in the same square each occupy one corner of the shared space, producing the anti-aliased look that softens diagonal lines in charted designs.
sourceNotes: Therese de Dillmont, Encyclopedia of Needlework (1886), Project Gutenberg #20776. Fractional stitch technique is documented in the major cross-stitch publisher guides from the 1980s onward.

content.text: When a chart shows two different symbols in the same square divided diagonally, the square is shared between a
. Together they fill the square with two colours. At a distance the combination reads as a smooth diagonal edge between the two.
The two stitches share the centre hole of the

square as their common destination. The three-quarter occupies more of the square and should be worked first; the quarter then fills the remaining corner. On most charts the three-quarter is the dominant colour in the shared square and the quarter is the contrasting edge colour.

A shared square on a chart shows two triangles, each filled with a different pattern symbol. The larger triangle is the three-quarter stitch; the smaller is the quarter stitch. The diagonal between them runs either from top-left to bottom-right (the forward slash /) or from top-right to bottom-left (the backslash). This diagonal is the boundary between the two stitches.
How to work the shared square

Thread the three-quarter colour first. Work the three-quarter cross-stitch: come up at the bottom-left, take the lower diagonal to the top-right, come back up at the top-left, and take the half-diagonal back down to the centre hole.
Thread the quarter colour. Work the quarter stitch: come up at the bottom-right and take the half-diagonal down to the same centre hole the three-quarter used.
Both stitches share the centre hole. The three-quarter sits on top at the centre; the quarter fills the remaining corner. Pull both with the same light tension.

items.symptom: The two stitches in the shared square overlap and one covers the other
items.cause: The three-quarter was worked after the quarter, or the strands are too many for the square size.
items.fix: Always work the three-quarter first, then the quarter. On very fine fabric counts (18-count or above) reduce the strand count to one strand for fractional stitches.

items.symptom: The shared square looks no different from a full cross
items.cause: Both stitches are in the same colour.
items.fix: Check the chart key. If the two triangles in the shared square have the same symbol, they may both be the same colour and the square is intended to be a full cross (sometimes charts print fractional symbols for a single colour as a visual artefact of the rendering).

content.text: Fractional stitches are most visible on curved outlines, animal fur edges, and petal boundaries. The next step is applying them in a project where a curved subject (a cat silhouette, a round flower head) calls for a smooth diagonal edge in the chart.

glossaryTerms.definition: A half-diagonal stitch from one corner of an Aida square to its centre. Pairs with three-quarter cross in the same square to break a colour boundary across the middle of a cell.
A full diagonal plus a half-diagonal back to the centre of the square. Used at edges and curves to soften the stepped look a full-cross-only chart gives.

A stiff, evenly-woven cross-stitch fabric with clearly visible squares formed by groups of threads. The default for beginners. Counted in squares per inch: 11ct, 14ct, 16ct, and 18ct are the common counts.
